questions.title: What plagiarism is
questions.text: Which statement best defines **plagiarism**?

options.content: Using a source and giving a full reference to it
Presenting another person's work or ideas as your own without acknowledging the source
Copying a file to a USB drive as a backup
Breaking into a computer system without permission

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Plagiarism = someone else's work presented as yours, without acknowledging the source. Using a source with a reference is fine.

questions.title: Forms of plagiarism
questions.text: Match each situation to the form of plagiarism.

left.text: A paragraph is copied from a website without quotation marks or a reference
A student changes the variable names in a friend's program and submits it
A student submits last year's project again for a new task
An English article is translated into Kazakh and presented as original

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Copying without quotes = direct; renamed variables = code; re-submitting own work = self-plagiarism; translating = translation plagiarism.

questions.title: Name the form
questions.text: A student takes sentences from three websites, changes a few words in each and joins them into one paragraph with no references. Which form of plagiarism is this?

options.content: Self-plagiarism
Mosaic plagiarism / patchwriting
Translation plagiarism
Incorrect citation

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Mixing phrases from several sources with a few words changed is mosaic plagiarism (patchwriting).

questions.title: Paraphrasing
questions.text: If you rewrite someone else's idea in your own words, you do not need to cite the source.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A paraphrase still uses another person's idea, so the source must be cited.

questions.title: Why plagiarism is a problem
questions.text: Select the **two** reasons why plagiarism is a problem.

options.content: It is unfair to the original author
It makes the document file larger
The student does not develop the skills the task was set for
It slows down the school network
It always damages the computer

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Plagiarism is dishonest and unfair to the author and other students, and the student does not learn.

questions.title: Order of checking
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

The text of the document is compared with a large [[1]] of sources. Matching fragments are [[2]] in the report. The report also shows a similarity score as a [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) database (2) highlighted (3) percentage
scheme.explanation: The document is compared with a database; matches are highlighted; a similarity percentage is calculated.

questions.title: Anti-plagiarism resources
questions.text: Select **two** resources used to check documents for plagiarism.

options.content: Turnitin
Microsoft Excel
Antiplagiat
Windows Defender

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Turnitin and Antiplagiat compare documents with databases of texts. Excel and Windows Defender do not.

questions.title: What the checker compares with
questions.text: Select the **three** collections an institutional anti-plagiarism service compares a document with.

options.content: Web pages
The student's browser history
Books and journal articles
Previously submitted student papers
The teacher's mark book

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Checkers use indexed web pages, publications and their own archive of submitted work.

questions.title: Similarity score
questions.text: What does the **similarity score** in an anti-plagiarism report show?

options.content: The percentage of the document that is plagiarised
The percentage of the document's text that matches text in the checker's databases
The number of spelling mistakes
The mark the teacher should give

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: It measures matching text only. Quoted and cited passages and the reference list also match, so a person must decide.

questions.title: A score of 0 %
questions.text: A similarity score of 0 % proves that a document contains no plagiarism.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Text copied from sources outside the database, or heavily paraphrased or translated text, may not be detected.

questions.title: Checking program code
questions.text: A teacher wants to find out whether two students handed in the same program with only the variable names changed. Which resource is designed for this?

options.content: MOSS
Microsoft Word spell checker
A search engine image search
A file compression tool

scheme.mark_scheme: A.
scheme.explanation: MOSS and JPlag compare the structure of program code, so renaming variables does not hide copying.

questions.title: Free checker
questions.text: Aliya copies a section of a classmate's report. Her teacher checks it with a **free online checker** and finds no match. What is the most likely reason?

options.content: Free checkers do not accept DOCX files
The classmate's report is not in the free checker's database, which mostly contains public web pages
Free checkers only check spelling
The copied section was too short to read

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Institutional services keep an archive of submitted papers; free checkers mostly search public web pages.

questions.title: Judge each match
questions.text: A similarity report highlights four passages in a student's report. Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: A definition in quotation marks with the author, year and page
A paragraph copied from a website with no quotation marks or reference
The entries of the reference list
A section that matches a paper another student submitted last year

scheme.mark_scheme: A definition in quotation marks with the author, year and page — Acceptable (1); A paragraph copied from a website with no quotation marks or reference — Plagiarism (1); The entries of the reference list — Acceptable (1); A section that matches a paper another student submitted last year — Plagiarism (1)
scheme.model_answer: A definition in quotation marks with the author, year and page — Acceptable; A paragraph copied from a website with no quotation marks or reference — Plagiarism; The entries of the reference list — Acceptable; A section that matches a paper another student submitted last year — Plagiarism.
scheme.explanation: Quoted and cited text and the reference list are acceptable matches; uncredited copying from a website or another student is plagiarism.

questions.title: Limitations
questions.text: Select the **two** limitations of anti-plagiarism software.

options.content: It cannot find copying from sources that are not in its database
It always shows the student's name
Heavily paraphrased or translated text may not be detected
It can only check documents shorter than one page
It cannot highlight matching text

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: A checker only finds what is in its databases, and rewriting or translation can hide copying. Highlighting matches is its main feature.

questions.title: Exclude the quotations
questions.text:
A report shows a similarity of **25 %**: 12 % from a website (copied, no quotation marks), 9 % from another student's paper and 4 % from a correctly quoted and cited textbook passage. The teacher turns on the filter **exclude quotes**.

Calculate the new similarity percentage (number only).

scheme.explanation: Only the quoted 4 % is removed: 25 − 4 = 21 %. The other matches are not in quotation marks.

questions.title: Fixing a highlighted passage
questions.text: Checking her own report, Dana sees a highlighted passage that is **her paraphrase** of an article, but she gave **no citation**. What should she do?

options.content: Nothing — a paraphrase is her own work
Add a citation to the article (and check the wording is really her own)
Delete the reference list
Replace words with synonyms until the highlighting disappears

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: A paraphrase uses someone else's idea, so it needs a citation; synonym-swapping is patchwriting.

questions.title: Checking with a search engine
questions.text: How can a teacher quickly check whether one suspicious sentence was copied from the web without an anti-plagiarism service?

options.content: Count the words in the sentence
Search the exact sentence in quotation marks in a search engine
Run a virus scan
Print the document

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Quotation marks make the search engine look for the exact phrase.

questions.title: Checking your own document
questions.text:
Complete the advice.

Before submitting, upload your final draft to an anti-plagiarism resource. Open every [[1]] passage. If it is a quotation, add quotation [[2]] and a reference. Make sure every source is in the reference [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) highlighted (2) marks (3) list

questions.title: Quotation
questions.text: What is a **quotation**?

options.content: The main points of a text in your own words
The exact words of a source in quotation marks, with a citation
A list of sources at the end of a document
A translation of a text

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: A quotation copies the exact words, so they must be in quotation marks and cited.

questions.title: Quote or paraphrase
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: The exact words of the author in quotation marks
The author's idea rewritten in your own words, about the same length
The main points of a long article in a few sentences

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Quotation (1); 2 Paraphrase (1); 3 Summary (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Quotation; 2 Paraphrase; 3 Summary.
scheme.explanation: Quotation = exact words; paraphrase = idea in own words, similar length; summary = main points, much shorter.

questions.title: Does it need a citation?
questions.text: Select the **two** statements in a student's report that **need a citation**.

options.content: Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan
62 % of Kazakhstan's schools used online diaries in 2025
Water boils at 100 °C at sea level
An expert's opinion that AI will replace most help-desk staff
A computer needs electricity to work

scheme.mark_scheme: B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Statistics and opinions come from a specific source; widely known facts are common knowledge.

questions.title: Harvard citations
questions.text:
Complete the sentences about Harvard-style referencing.

In the text, a citation gives the author's surname and the [[1]] of publication, e.g. (Connolly and Begg, 2015). The full details of every source are given in the reference [[2]], in [[3]] order of authors' surnames.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) year (2) list (3) alphabetical

questions.title: A correct paraphrase
questions.text:
Original (Sadykova, 2024): *"Backing up data to a second location protects a small business from losing its records after a fire or theft."*

Which is a correct paraphrase?

options.content: Backing up data to a second location protects a small business from losing its records after a fire or theft.
Backing up information to another location protects a small firm from losing its records after a fire or robbery.
Keeping a copy of its data somewhere else lets a small firm recover if its office burns or is robbed (Sadykova, 2024).
Keeping a copy of its data somewhere else lets a small firm recover if its office burns or is robbed.

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: A is copied; B only swaps synonyms (patchwriting); D is a good rewording but has no citation; C is reworded and cited.

questions.title: Registration
questions.text: A student's essay is only protected by copyright if it is registered with the state.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Copyright arises automatically when an original work is created; no registration or © sign is needed.

questions.title: Copyright
questions.text: Which statement best defines **copyright**?

options.content: The right of anyone to copy material found on the Internet
The exclusive legal right of the author of an original work to copy, distribute and adapt it and to allow others to do so
A password that protects a document
A rule that all software must be free

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Copyright gives the author / owner control over copying, distribution and adaptation.

questions.title: How long it lasts
questions.text: In Kazakhstan, copyright normally lasts for the author's life plus how many years? (number only)

scheme.explanation: Life + 70 years; then the work enters the public domain.

questions.title: Copyright terms
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Permission to use a work under stated conditions
The right to earn money from copies and licences
Works no longer protected that anyone may use
The right to be named as the author and to protect the work from distortion

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R2, L2–R4, L3–R1, L4–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Creative Commons
questions.text: Match each Creative Commons element to its meaning.

right.text: Changed versions must use the same licence
You may not change the work

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R3, L2–R2, L3–R4, L4–R1. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Allowed or not
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each use is allowed under copyright rules.

prefill: Quoting two sentences from a book in an essay, with the author and page
Installing a copy of paid software borrowed from a friend
Using a CC BY photo in a school poster and crediting the photographer
Selling copies of a film downloaded from the Internet

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Allowed (1); 2 Not allowed (1); 3 Allowed (1); 4 Not allowed (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Allowed; 2 Not allowed; 3 Allowed; 4 Not allowed.
scheme.explanation: Short cited quotations and CC BY with credit are allowed; unlicensed software copies and selling films break copyright.

questions.title: Ideas
questions.text: Copyright protects an idea itself, so nobody else may write about the same idea.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Copyright protects the expression of an idea (the text, code, image), not the idea or the facts.

questions.title: What a licence does
questions.text: A school buys a licence for 30 copies of a design program. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The school now owns the copyright of the program
The school may install it on 30 computers under the licence conditions
The school may sell copies to other schools
The school may install it on any number of computers

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: A licence is permission under conditions; it does not transfer ownership.

questions.title: Using a CC image
questions.text: An image is licensed **CC BY-NC-ND**. Which use is allowed?

options.content: Cropping it and using it in a paid advertisement
Using it unchanged on a school club website with the author credited
Using it unchanged in a paid app without credit
Editing the colours and sharing it with credit

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: BY = credit, NC = non-commercial, ND = no changes. Only B meets all three.

questions.title: Plagiarism or copyright infringement
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: A poem by Abai (died 1904) is copied into an essay without naming the author
A company sells copies of a recent film and names the director on the cover
A blogger copies a recent magazine article and publishes it as their own

scheme.mark_scheme: A poem by Abai (died 1904) is copied into an essay without naming the author — Plagiarism only (1); A company sells copies of a recent film and names the director on the cover — Copyright infringement only (1); A blogger copies a recent magazine article and publishes it as their own — Both (1)
scheme.model_answer: A poem by Abai (died 1904) is copied into an essay without naming the author — Plagiarism only; A company sells copies of a recent film and names the director on the cover — Copyright infringement only; A blogger copies a recent magazine article and publishes it as their own — Both.
scheme.explanation: Abai's work is in the public domain, so there is no copyright problem — but hiding the author is plagiarism. Selling copies without permission infringes copyright even with credit. Copying and claiming a protected article is both.

questions.title: No longer protected
questions.text: State the term for works whose copyright has expired, so that anyone may use them freely.

scheme.mark_scheme: public domain
scheme.explanation: After the term of protection ends, a work enters the public domain.

questions.title: Checking Madina's project report
questions.text: Madina, a Grade 12 student, writes a report about smart home systems for her project documentation. Her teacher checks every report with the school's anti-plagiarism resource.

parts.title: Plagiarism
parts.text: Define the term **plagiarism**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- presenting another person's work / words / ideas / code as your own (1)
- without acknowledging / citing the source (1)
scheme.model_answer: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own without acknowledging the source.

parts.title: Forms of plagiarism
parts.text: Draw a line to link each thing a student might do to the form of plagiarism.

left.text: An English article is translated into Kazakh and handed in as original
Sentences from several websites are joined with a few words changed
The student hands in her own essay from last year for a new task

scheme.mark_scheme: Kazakh translation of an English article – translation plagiarism; sentences from several sites with words changed – mosaic / patchwriting; last year's own essay re-submitted – self-plagiarism (1 each)
scheme.model_answer: 1 → Translation plagiarism; 2 → Mosaic plagiarism; 3 → Self-plagiarism

parts.title: How the checker works
parts.text: Describe how the anti-plagiarism resource checks Madina's report.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the text is split into fragments / fingerprints (1)
- compared with a large database of web pages / publications / previously submitted work (1)
- matching parts are highlighted with their sources and a similarity percentage / report is produced (1)
scheme.model_answer: The report is uploaded and split into fragments that are fingerprinted; these are compared with a database of web pages, publications and submitted papers; matches are highlighted with links to their sources and a similarity percentage is given.

parts.title: Consequences
parts.text: State **two** consequences for a student who is found to have plagiarised.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): zero / reduced marks; work must be redone; disqualification from the exam / competition; loss of reputation / trust; expulsion; legal action for copyright infringement
scheme.model_answer: 1 Zero marks for the work. 2 Disqualification from the exam.

questions.title: Reading a similarity report
questions.text:
Arman's report on network security receives this similarity report:

| Source | Match |
|---|---|
| 1. A news website — paragraph copied, no quotation marks | 14 % |
| 2. A textbook — two sentences in quotation marks with author, year and page | 6 % |
| 3. Arman's reference list | 5 % |
| 4. A report submitted by a student at another school in 2025 | 7 % |
| **Total similarity** | **32 %** |

parts.title: Originality
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of Arman's report that is **original** (number only).

parts.title: The score is not proof
parts.text: Explain why a similarity of 32 % does **not** on its own prove that Arman has plagiarised.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- some matches are acceptable: quoted and cited text / the reference list / common phrases (1)
- the score only shows matching text; a person must check each match to decide (1)
scheme.model_answer: Sources 2 and 3 are a correctly quoted passage and his own reference list, which are acceptable; the score only measures matching text, so the teacher must look at each match.

parts.title: Judge each source
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box for each source in the report.

prefill: 1 News website
2 Textbook
3 Reference list
4 Another student's report

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Plagiarism (1); 2 Acceptable (1); 3 Acceptable (1); 4 Plagiarism (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Plagiarism; 2 Acceptable; 3 Acceptable; 4 Plagiarism

parts.title: Limitations
parts.text: The school also uses a free online checker, which gave Arman's report only 15 %. Explain **three** limitations of anti-plagiarism software, one of which explains the lower score.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each), one linked to the free checker: smaller database / no archive of submitted papers, so source 4 (another student's report) is not found; cannot find sources not in its database (printed books); heavy paraphrasing / translation may not be detected; false positives from common phrases / references; does not check images / ideas
scheme.model_answer: 1 The free checker mostly searches public web pages and has no archive of submitted papers, so the other student's report was not found. 2 Paraphrased or translated text may not be detected. 3 Common phrases and the reference list give false positives.

questions.title: Writing the documentation without plagiarism
questions.text: Students of a Shymkent school are writing the user guide for a library system they developed. They use a textbook, two websites and a journal article.

parts.title: Quotation and paraphrase
parts.text: Compare a **quotation** and a **paraphrase**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a quotation uses the exact words of the source in quotation marks (1)
- a paraphrase restates the idea in your own words / structure (1) [both need a citation]
scheme.model_answer: A quotation copies the author's exact words in quotation marks; a paraphrase rewrites the idea in the student's own words. Both must be cited.

parts.title: Why cite a paraphrase
parts.text: Explain why a paraphrase still needs a citation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the idea / information belongs to another author (1)
- without a citation it is presented as the student's own idea, which is plagiarism (1)
scheme.model_answer: Although the words are new, the idea comes from the source; without a citation the student presents it as their own, which is plagiarism.

parts.title: How to paraphrase
parts.text: Describe how a student should paraphrase a paragraph from the journal article correctly.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): read until the meaning is understood; close the source and write the idea from memory in own words and sentence structure; compare with the original to check no phrases are copied and the meaning is unchanged; put any kept phrase in quotation marks; add the citation (author, year)
scheme.model_answer: Read the paragraph until it is understood, close the article and write the idea in your own words and structure, then compare with the original and add the citation (author, year).

parts.title: Reference list
parts.text: State **three** items of information that a reference list entry for one of the **websites** should contain.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): author / organisation; year of publication; title of the page; URL / web address; date accessed
scheme.model_answer: 1 Author or organisation  2 Title of the page  3 URL and date accessed

questions.title: Copyright in a new mobile app
questions.text: **Qadam**, a start-up in Almaty, is developing a **paid** fitness app. The developers want to use photographs and music found online and some open-source code.

parts.title: Copyright
parts.text: Define the term **copyright**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the exclusive legal right of the author / owner of an original work (1)
- to copy / distribute / adapt / publish it and to allow or forbid others to do so (1)
scheme.model_answer: Copyright is the author's exclusive legal right to copy, distribute and adapt their original work and to decide who else may do so.

parts.title: Copyright rules
parts.text: Name **three** rules of copyright protection.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): protection is automatic / no registration needed; the author has economic and moral rights; protection lasts for a limited time (life + 70 years) then public domain; copying / publishing needs the owner's permission or a licence; ideas and facts are not protected, only their expression; limited free use (quotation with author and source); software is protected like a literary work
scheme.model_answer: 1 Copyright is automatic from creation. 2 Using the work needs the owner's permission or a licence. 3 Protection lasts for the author's life + 70 years.

parts.title: A CC BY-NC photo
parts.text: One photograph has a **CC BY-NC** licence. Explain whether Qadam may use it in the app.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- not allowed / they may not (1)
- NC means non-commercial use only and the app is sold / commercial (so they need the owner's permission or another licence) (1)
scheme.model_answer: No: NC allows only non-commercial use, and Qadam's app is paid, so they must ask the photographer for permission or buy a licence.

parts.title: Plagiarism and copyright
parts.text: Explain the difference between **plagiarism** and **copyright infringement**, using an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- plagiarism: presenting another's work as your own / not acknowledging the source — an ethical / academic offence (1)
- copyright infringement: using a protected work without the owner's permission / licence — a legal offence, even with credit (1)
- a suitable example (e.g. using music in the app with the artist credited but without a licence = infringement, not plagiarism) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Plagiarism means not acknowledging the source and claiming the work; infringement means using a protected work without permission. If Qadam used a song and credited the artist but had no licence, it would be infringement, not plagiarism.

questions.title: Timur's technical documentation and the school checker
questions.text:
Timur, a Grade 12 student in Kostanay, is writing the technical documentation for **Saqta**, a database app he developed for a local shop. His school checks every project document with an institutional anti-plagiarism resource that stores all submitted work in its archive.

The checker cuts the text into overlapping fragments of **3 words** (shingles) and compares their fingerprints. One sentence of a web source and one sentence of Timur's document are:

- **Source:** *an index makes searching a large table much faster*
- **Timur:** *an index makes searching a big table much faster*

parts.title: Deliberate or accidental
parts.text: Explain the difference between **deliberate** and **accidental** plagiarism, giving an example of each.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- deliberate: the student knowingly copies / presents another person's work as their own, e.g. pasting a paragraph from a website or submitting a classmate's code (1)
- accidental: the student does not intend to, e.g. forgets where a note came from / loses the quotation marks / does not know how to paraphrase or cite (1)
scheme.model_answer: Deliberate plagiarism is done on purpose — for example copying a section from a website to save time. Accidental plagiarism happens without intending it — for example forgetting which source a note came from, so the copied sentence appears without a citation.

parts.title: A form of plagiarism
parts.text: Timur finds a good description of indexing in a Russian article, translates it into English and puts it in his document without a reference. Which form of plagiarism is this?

scheme.model_answer: B — translation plagiarism.
scheme.explanation: Translating a text does not make it yours: the ideas and their order still belong to the author, and no source is given.

options.content: Self-plagiarism
Translation plagiarism
Incorrect citation
Code plagiarism

parts.title: Counting fingerprints
parts.text: Using 3-word fragments, state:

fields.label: the number of fragments in the source sentence
the number of these fragments that also appear in Timur's sentence

scheme.model_answer: Source fragments: an index makes / index makes searching / makes searching a / searching a large / a large table / large table much / table much faster = 7. Matching in Timur's sentence: an index makes, index makes searching, makes searching a, table much faster = 4.

parts.title: Changing one word
parts.text: Explain why changing *large* to *big* did **not** hide the copying from the checker.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- only the fragments that contain the changed word stop matching (here 3 of 7) (1)
- the other overlapping fragments still match in a row, so the checker still highlights the passage and links it to the source (1)

points.criterion: Only fragments with the changed word break
Remaining fragments still match / passage highlighted

scheme.model_answer: Because the fragments overlap, changing one word breaks only the three fragments that contain it. The other four still have identical fingerprints, so the checker still finds the matching run of text and highlights it with its source.

parts.title: Copying from a classmate
parts.text: Timur's friend copied two pages from Timur's document, which had been submitted a week earlier. Explain why the school's checker can find this copying but a free online checker probably cannot.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the institutional checker stores submitted documents in its archive, so the friend's text is compared with Timur's submitted document and matches (1)
- a free checker mostly compares with public web pages; Timur's document is not on the web / not in its database, so it finds no match (1)

points.criterion: Free checker: web only, document not in its database

scheme.model_answer: The school's service keeps every submitted document in its archive, so the friend's pages match Timur's earlier submission. A free checker mostly searches the public web; Timur's document is not published there, so it is not in its database and no match is found.

questions.title: Dana's similarity report
questions.text:
Dana checks her 15-page project report before submitting it. The similarity report shows **28 %** overall:

| Source | Match | What Dana's report contains |
|---|---|---|
| 1. An online encyclopedia | 13 % | A definition copied word for word, with no quotation marks and no reference |
| 2. A report submitted by a student in 2025 | 8 % | A section rewritten from her cousin's report, with some words changed |
| 3. A national standard on documentation | 4 % | A short passage in quotation marks, with a citation and a reference list entry |
| 4. Several sources | 3 % | Her reference list |

parts.title: Originality
parts.text: Calculate the **originality** of Dana's report as a percentage.

scheme.model_answer: Originality = 100 − 28 = 72 %.

parts.title: Using the filters
parts.text: Dana switches on the filters *exclude quotes* and *exclude bibliography*. Calculate the similarity score that is now shown.

scheme.model_answer: 28 − 4 (quotation) − 3 (reference list) = 21 %.

parts.title: Judging the matches
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box for each source to show whether the match is acceptable or must be corrected.

prefill: 1. Online encyclopedia
2. Student report from 2025
3. National standard
4. Reference list

scheme.mark_scheme:
Source 1 – must be corrected (1)
Source 2 – must be corrected (1)
Source 3 – acceptable (1)
Source 4 – acceptable (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 must be corrected (copied without quotation marks or citation); 2 must be corrected (another student's work, patchwriting); 3 acceptable (correctly quoted and cited); 4 acceptable (a reference list always matches).

parts.title: Correcting source 1
parts.text: Describe **two** different ways in which Dana could correct the passage from source 1.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- put the exact words in quotation marks and add a citation (author, year) and a reference list entry (1)

summary: What plagiarism is and its forms, how anti-plagiarism resources check documents (fragments, fingerprints, databases, code checkers, similarity report), how to check your own document and read a report, the limits of these tools, how to avoid plagiarism by quoting, paraphrasing and citing, and the main rules of copyright protection (why copyright exists, automatic protection, economic and moral rights, term, permission and licences, free use, plagiarism vs infringement) and software licences (EULA, proprietary, shareware, freeware, open source, copyleft and permissive, piracy).

blocks.content: When students write documentation for a project — a report, a user guide, a technical description — they use many sources: web pages, books, other people's code. Using sources is normal and good; **hiding** that you used them is **plagiarism**.

In grade 12 this topic belongs to **creating documentation**. A system that is developed for a client is delivered with documents: a **technical specification**, a **user guide**, a **test report**, a **project report** for the school. These documents are judged as **your** work — by a teacher, an examiner or a client who pays for them. If parts of them were written by someone else and this is not shown, the reader is misled about what you did and what you know. That is why checking documents for plagiarism is part of producing professional documentation, not only a school rule.

There is nothing wrong with **using** sources. Every good report builds on other people's work: a definition from a textbook, a statistic from a government website, a code example from the documentation of a library. The difference between research and plagiarism is **acknowledgement**. When the reader can see **which** words or ideas came from **which** source, the work is honest; when the borrowed material is mixed in without a sign, it is plagiarism — even if the writer did not mean to cheat.

Plagiarism can be **deliberate** (copying a whole essay to save time) or **accidental** (forgetting where a note came from, or not knowing how to paraphrase). Schools and universities usually treat both seriously, because the result for the reader is the same: the work is not what it claims to be. The best protection against accidental plagiarism is **good habits while researching** — recording every source and marking copied text in your notes — and **checking the final document** before handing it in.

Plagiarism is not only about words. A diagram redrawn from a website, a table of data, a photograph, a piece of music in a video, a program, even the **structure** of someone else's argument can all be plagiarised. Translating a text from Russian or English into Kazakh does not make it yours either: the ideas and the order of the content still belong to the original author.

**Presenting another person's work, words, ideas, images or code as your own**, without clearly **acknowledging the source**. It is a form of **academic dishonesty** and can also break **copyright** law.

A **source** is any work you take information from (book, article, web page, video, program). A **citation (reference)** tells the reader **who** created the source, **when**, and **where** to find it.
Doing your work **honestly**: your own words and ideas, with **every source acknowledged**, and following the rules of the task (e.g. whether AI tools or help from others are allowed).

blocks.title: Forms of plagiarism
rows: Text is copied **word for word** without quotation marks or a reference
A paragraph from Wikipedia pasted into an essay
Phrases from several sources are **mixed** together with a few words changed
Sentences from three websites stitched together
Someone else's **idea** is rewritten in new words, but the source is **not given**
An article's argument retold with no reference
A text in another language is **translated** and presented as original
An English article translated into Kazakh
Re-using **your own earlier work** without permission or acknowledgement
Last year's project submitted for a new task
Copying program code and only changing **variable names / comments**
A classmate's Python game with renamed variables
Work written by **another person** or an **AI tool** submitted as your own, when this is not allowed
An essay generated by a chatbot
A **wrong or incomplete** source, so the reader cannot find the original

blocks.content: The forms differ in **how much** is taken and **how well it is hidden**, but they all share one feature: the reader is not told the truth about the source. Direct copying is the easiest to detect; mosaic plagiarism and translation are harder, because the exact words have changed. Self-plagiarism surprises many students: you are allowed to build on your own earlier work, but you must say that you are doing so, and you must have the teacher's agreement if the task asks for **new** work.

items.title: Why plagiarism is a problem
items.content:
- It is **dishonest** — the work does not show the student's own knowledge.
- It is **unfair** to the original author and to other students.
- The student **does not learn** the skills the task was designed to develop.
- It can **break copyright** — the author's rights are ignored.

items.title: Consequences
items.content:
- At school: **zero marks**, the work must be redone, a note to parents.
- In exams and competitions: **disqualification**.
- At university: a failed course or **expulsion**; degrees can be withdrawn.
- At work: **loss of reputation**, dismissal, **legal action** for copyright infringement.

items.title: Why people plagiarise
items.content:
- Lack of time / poor planning.
- Not knowing how to **cite** or **paraphrase** correctly.
- Thinking that information on the Internet is **free to use**.
- Pressure to get high marks.

blocks.content:
- "I changed some words, so it is mine" — it is still **patchwriting / plagiarism** without a citation.
- "It was on the Internet, so anyone can use it" — web content is **protected by copyright** too.
- Forgetting that **ideas, images, tables and code** can be plagiarised, not only text.
- Thinking that re-using your **own** old work is always fine — without permission it is **self-plagiarism**.

A program or online service that **compares a document with a very large database of texts** — web pages, books, journals and previously submitted student work — and produces a **similarity report** showing **which parts match other sources** and **how much** of the document matches.
The **percentage of the document's text that matches** text in the checker's databases. **Originality** = 100 % − similarity. It measures **matching text**, not plagiarism.

A teacher who marks 60 reports cannot remember every web page, book and earlier student paper on the topic. A computer can store **billions** of documents and compare a new text with all of them in seconds. Anti-plagiarism resources therefore do the part of the job that computers are good at — **finding matching text quickly in a huge collection** — and leave the part that needs judgement — **deciding whether the matching is acceptable** — to a person.

Comparing a whole document with millions of others word by word would be far too slow. Checkers therefore **normalise** the text first: they convert it to lower case, remove punctuation and often remove very common words ("the", "and", "of"). Then they cut it into **overlapping fragments** of a fixed number of words, called **shingles** (n-grams). Each fragment is turned by a **hash function** into a short number, its **fingerprint**. Two identical fragments always give the same fingerprint, so finding matching text becomes the fast job of finding **equal numbers** in an index — just as a library catalogue finds a book by its code without reading every shelf.

Because the fragments **overlap**, copying even one sentence produces several matching fingerprints in a row, and the checker can mark the whole copied passage. Changing a single word breaks only the fragments that contain that word; the others still match. That is why "changing a few words" rarely hides copying. Some modern checkers also compare **meaning**, not just exact words, so that synonyms and reordered sentences can be detected, and some can compare a text with sources in **other languages**.

A checker can only find a match with a text that is in its **databases**. These are usually of three kinds: **the public Internet** (crawled web pages), **published material** (books, journals, conference papers, often through agreements with publishers) and an **archive of documents submitted before** to that service. The archive is the reason institutional services can find copying between students: when a student submits a report, it is stored, and next year's copy of it will match. Free online checkers usually search only the web, so they cannot see a classmate's work or a printed book.

Program code is checked differently. Renaming variables, changing comments or reordering functions does not change what a program **does**, so code checkers such as **MOSS** and **JPlag** first convert the program into a sequence of **tokens** (keyword, identifier, operator, number…) and compare the **structure**, not the names. Two programs that differ only in variable names give the same token sequence and are reported as similar.

blocks.title: How a document is checked
items: The user (or teacher) **uploads** the document (DOCX, PDF, TXT) or pastes the text.
The system breaks the text into **fragments** (overlapping sequences of words, "shingles") and creates a **digital fingerprint (hash)** of each.
The fingerprints are **compared** with its databases: the Internet, academic publications, its **archive of submitted papers**.
**Matching fragments are highlighted**, and each match is linked to its **source**.
A **similarity (originality) score** in % is calculated, and a **report** is produced for the user to **interpret**.

blocks.title: Worked example — how fingerprints find a copied sentence
blocks.content:
*A source on the web contains the sentence* "A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table". *A student's report contains* "In our database a primary key uniquely identifies every record in a table".

1. **Normalise** both: lower case, no punctuation → *a primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table* and *in our database a primary key uniquely identifies every record in a table*.
2. **Shingles of 3 words** from the source: *a primary key*, *primary key uniquely*, *key uniquely identifies*, *uniquely identifies each*, *identifies each record*, *each record in*, *record in a*, *in a table*.
3. **Shingles of the report** include *a primary key*, *primary key uniquely*, *key uniquely identifies*, *record in a*, *in a table* — **5 of the 8** source fingerprints match. The shingles containing *every* (instead of *each*) do not match.
4. The checker **highlights** the passage and links it to the web page. Changing one word did **not** hide the copying.
5. The teacher looks at the passage: there are no quotation marks and no reference, so it must be **quoted with a citation or rewritten and cited**.

blocks.text: What the checker can and cannot do

blocks.content: An anti-plagiarism resource is a **tool for finding evidence**, not a judge. Its strengths are speed, the size of its databases and the fact that it treats every document in the same way. Its weaknesses come from the way it works: it can only match text that is **already in its databases**, it compares **words and fragments** rather than understanding ideas, and it cannot know the **rules of the task** — whether a quotation was allowed, whether the student worked in a permitted group, whether a passage is the student's own earlier work used with permission. A report must therefore always be **interpreted by a person** who knows the task and the student. Teachers use the report as a starting point for a conversation, for example by asking the student to explain a highlighted passage in their own words.

items.title: Limitations of anti-plagiarism software
items.content:
- Cannot detect copying from **sources not in its database** (printed books, private documents).
- Can be fooled by heavy **paraphrasing**, synonym-replacing tools or **translation**.
- Does not check **images, diagrams** or **ideas** well.
- **False positives** — common phrases, names, standard definitions, the reference list.
- Uploaded work may be **stored** by the service — privacy of the student's own work.
- A human must always **interpret** the report.

items.title: What the checker cannot decide
items.content:
- Whether a match is **properly quoted and cited**.
- Whether the use is **allowed** by the task rules.
- Whether the student **understood** the work.

theory.title: Checking a document and reading the report

blocks.content: The main purpose of checking your **own** document is to catch problems **before** someone else does. Students often discover that a sentence they thought was their own is almost identical to a website they read weeks ago, or that a quotation lost its quotation marks when it was pasted. A check gives time to correct these honestly.

blocks.text: The parts of a similarity report

blocks.content: Most reports have the same parts. The **overall similarity score** in per cent is shown at the top. Below it is a **list of sources**, each with its own percentage — the share of the document that matches that one source — usually in order from the largest. The **document itself** is shown with matching passages **highlighted**, often in a different colour for each source, so you can click a passage and see the original next to it. **Filters** let you exclude quoted text, the bibliography and very short matches (for example, fewer than 8 words), and the score is recalculated. Some services also show an **AI-writing indicator**; like the similarity score, it is a signal to investigate, not proof.

Reading a report means asking the same three questions about every highlighted passage. **Is it acknowledged?** A quotation in quotation marks with a reference is honest, even if it matches 100 %. **Is it necessary?** A report that is 40 % correct quotations is honest but shows little of the student's own work, and may get a low mark for that reason. **Is it common language?** Phrases such as "the aim of this project is" or standard technical terms match many sources and are not plagiarism. Only matches that are **not acknowledged** and **not common language** are real problems.

blocks.title: Checking your own document before submitting
items: Finish the **final draft**, with all quotations in **quotation marks** and a full **reference list**.
Upload it to the school's checker (or a free one) and wait for the **report**.
Look at the **overall score**, then at **every highlighted passage** and its source.
Use the filters to **exclude quotations and the bibliography** — see what is left.
Fix every problem: add quotation marks and a reference to a quotation; **cite** a paraphrase; **rewrite** text that is too close to the source.
**Check again** and keep the final report.

blocks.title: Worked example — Aigerim's project report
blocks.content:
*Aigerim checks her 12-page project report with the school's checker. The report shows **25 %** similarity: 12 % from a Wikipedia article, 9 % from a student paper submitted last year, 4 % from her textbook.*

1. **Wikipedia, 12 %** — the passage is a definition she copied **without quotation marks**. She either puts it in **quotation marks with a reference** or **paraphrases** it in her own words **and cites** the article.
2. **Student paper, 9 %** — she remembers using her older brother's report. This is **plagiarism of another student's work**: she must **rewrite** the section herself.
3. **Textbook, 4 %** — a short quotation **already in quotation marks** and in the reference list. This is **acceptable**; the filter "exclude quotes" removes it from the score.
4. After the changes and a **second check** the similarity is **6 %**, made of common technical phrases and the reference list.

items.title: Interpreting the score correctly
items.content:
- A similarity score is **not** a plagiarism score — it only shows **matching text**.
- Correctly **quoted and referenced** passages, the **bibliography**, common phrases and technical terms also produce matches.
- Most checkers can **exclude quotes and the reference list** from the score.
- A **high score with no citations** needs investigation; a **low score** can still hide paraphrased or translated plagiarism.
- Many schools set a **threshold** (e.g. above 20–30 % is checked in detail), but every match is judged by a person.

items.title: Ways of checking without a dedicated service
items.content:
- Search a suspicious sentence **in quotation marks** in a search engine.
- Use **reverse image search** to find the source of a picture.
- Compare two programs with a **code-similarity tool** (MOSS, JPlag).
- Compare the **style** of a passage with the student's other work.

blocks.content:
- Treating the similarity % as **proof** of plagiarism, or 0 % as proof of originality.
- Using a synonym-replacer to "beat" the checker — the work is still plagiarised and often becomes unreadable.
- Checking only the **number** and never opening the highlighted passages.
- Uploading a confidential document to a free checker without reading its **privacy terms**.

theory.title: Exam practice: plagiarism and anti-plagiarism resources

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term plagiarism. [2]**
Presenting someone else's work / words / ideas as your own (1) without acknowledging / citing the source (1).

**Q: Describe how an anti-plagiarism resource checks a document. [3]**
The text is split into fragments / fingerprints (1); these are **compared with a large database** of web pages, publications and submitted work (1); **matching fragments are highlighted** with their sources and a **similarity percentage / report** is produced (1).

**Q: Explain why a similarity score of 25 % does not always mean that the student has plagiarised. [2]**
Matches may be **correctly quoted and cited** passages, the **reference list** or common phrases (1); the teacher must look at **which parts** match and whether they are acknowledged (1).

**Q: State two limitations of anti-plagiarism software. [2]**
Any two: cannot find sources not in its database (1); can be fooled by heavy paraphrasing / translation (1); false positives from common phrases; does not check images / ideas well.

**Q: Name a resource that can detect plagiarism in program code. [1]**
MOSS / JPlag (1).

- Saying the software "finds plagiarism" — it finds **matching text**; a human decides.
- Describing only "it checks the internet" — the mark needs **comparison with a database** and the **report / highlighting**.
- Giving "it is slow" or "it costs money" as a limitation — give a limitation of **detection**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define plagiarism and name five forms of it, with an example of each.
Explain why plagiarism is a problem and give two consequences.
Describe the steps an anti-plagiarism resource follows.
Name three anti-plagiarism resources, including one for program code.
Explain what a similarity score shows and why it is not a plagiarism score.
Give three limitations of anti-plagiarism software.

blocks.content: Avoiding plagiarism is a **skill**, not just a promise. It has three parts: deciding **how** to use each source (quote, paraphrase or summarise), **acknowledging** it in the text, and listing it in the **reference list** at the end. When all three are done, a reader — or an anti-plagiarism report — can separate your work from the work of others.

blocks.text: When to quote, paraphrase or summarise

blocks.content: **Quote** when the exact words matter: a legal definition, a striking statement, the words of an interview, a line of a standard. Quotations should be short and few; a report built from quotations shows that the writer collected material but did not process it. **Paraphrase** when you need one specific idea in detail but the original wording is not special — this is the most common choice in technical documentation, and it shows that you understood the source. **Summarise** when you need only the main points of a long text, such as the conclusion of a 20-page report in two sentences.

In every case the **citation** stays. Students often believe that once the words are their own, the source can be dropped. It cannot: the **idea, the data or the structure** still came from someone else. The only exception is **common knowledge** — facts that a typical reader knows or can find in many general sources without dispute. If you are unsure whether something is common knowledge, cite it; an extra citation is never plagiarism.

A **referencing style** is an agreed format for citations. In the **Harvard (author–date)** style the text contains the author's surname and the year in brackets, and the full details are in an alphabetical reference list. Other styles use **numbers** in square brackets [1] (IEEE, common in computing) or **footnotes**. The style matters less than **consistency** and **completeness**: the reader must be able to find the exact source. A web reference needs the author or organisation, year, title, URL and the **date you accessed it**, because web pages change. Word processors can build citations and the bibliography automatically from a list of sources, which keeps the two always matching.
The **exact words** of a source, placed in **quotation marks** (or indented for a long quotation), followed by a **citation**.

A **paraphrase** restates one idea **completely in your own words and sentence structure**; a **summary** gives only the **main points** of a longer text, much shorter. **Both still need a citation**, because the idea is not yours.
Facts that are **widely known** and found in many sources (e.g. "Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan"). They **do not need** a citation; statistics, opinions and specific findings do.

blocks.title: Citing a source (Harvard style)
blocks.content:
In the text: *Normalisation reduces data redundancy (Connolly and Begg, 2015).*

Every citation in the text has a matching entry in the **reference list**, which is in **alphabetical order** of authors.

blocks.title: Worked example — paraphrasing a passage step by step
blocks.content:
*Original (from a web page by the Ministry of Digital Development, 2025):* "Users should create passwords of at least twelve characters that combine upper- and lower-case letters, digits and symbols, and should never reuse the same password on different services."

1. **Bad (patchwriting):** "Users ought to make passwords of at least twelve characters that mix upper- and lower-case letters, numbers and symbols, and must not reuse a password on several services." — the structure and most words are copied; a checker would highlight it.
2. **Understand and close the source.** Main ideas: long password (12+), four kinds of character, a different password for each service.
3. **Write from memory:** "A strong password is long — twelve characters or more — and mixes the four kinds of character. Using a separate password for each account means that one leaked password does not open the others (Ministry of Digital Development, 2025)."
4. **Check:** the meaning is the same, the sentences are new (the student even added the reason), and the **citation** is present.
5. Add the full entry to the reference list.

blocks.title: How to paraphrase correctly
items: Read the passage until you **understand** it; then **close** the source.
Write the idea **from memory**, in your own words and your own sentence structure.
Compare with the original: no long phrases copied; the **meaning** is unchanged.
Put any unique phrase you kept in **quotation marks**.
Add the **citation** (author, year).

blocks.content: Keep a list of every source **while you research** (author, title, date, URL, date accessed), write notes **in your own words**, mark copied text in your notes clearly, and use the word processor's **References** tools (citations, bibliography, footnotes). Check your own document with an anti-plagiarism resource **before** you submit it.

- Quotation marks **without** a citation, or a citation **without** quotation marks around copied words.
- Swapping a few words for synonyms and calling it a paraphrase — that is **patchwriting**.
- A citation in the text that is **missing from the reference list**, or "Source: Google".
- Citing "common knowledge" for statistics or someone's opinion.

The **exclusive legal right of the author** (or owner) of an original work — text, software, music, images, films, websites — to **copy, distribute, adapt, publish and perform** it, and to **allow or forbid** others to do so.
**Permission from the copyright owner** to use a work under stated **conditions** (e.g. one computer, non-commercial use only, credit the author). It does **not** transfer ownership.
Works that are **no longer protected** by copyright (the term has expired) or whose owner gave up the rights. Anyone may use them freely.

blocks.title: The main rules of copyright protection
rows: A work is protected **from the moment it is created** in a material form — no registration is needed; the © sign is optional but useful
It is the author's **own creative work**, recorded in some form (written, saved, filmed)
**Economic rights** (to earn money from copies, licences) and **moral rights** (to be named as the author, to protect the work from distortion)
In Kazakhstan and many countries: the author's **life + 70 years**; afterwards the work enters the **public domain**
To copy, publish, translate, adapt or sell a work you need the **owner's permission** or a **licence**
Copyright protects the **expression** (the text, code, image), not the idea itself
**Quotation** for study, criticism, news or teaching is allowed **with the author's name and source** and only to a justified extent
**Software is protected like a literary work**
Copying, distributing or installing software without a **licence** is illegal
E.g. **Creative Commons**; open-source licences (GPL, MIT); a commercial **EULA**
Removal of content, fines, compensation to the owner, criminal liability in serious cases

blocks.content: Creating a program, a book or a song takes time, skill and money. If anybody could copy and sell it the moment it appeared, authors would have no way to earn from their work and fewer people would create. Copyright solves this by giving the author a **temporary monopoly**: for a limited time only the author (or whoever the author licenses) may make and sell copies. After that time the work passes into the **public domain** and becomes free for everyone, so society benefits too.

Copyright gives the author two groups of rights. **Economic (property) rights** concern money and control: the right to **reproduce** the work, **distribute** copies, **publish**, **translate**, **adapt**, **perform or show it publicly** and to **license** these actions to others for payment. Economic rights can be **sold or transferred** — a programmer employed by a company usually transfers the rights to the code to the employer. **Moral (personal) rights** belong to the author **personally** and cannot be sold: the right to be **named as the author** (attribution), the right to keep the work from being **distorted** in a way that harms the author's reputation, and the right to decide whether to publish it at all. That is why a software company can own the economic rights to a program, but the novelist always remains the author of the novel.

blocks.text: Free use — what is allowed without permission

blocks.content: The law allows some uses of protected works **without asking and without paying**, because they serve education, criticism or information. Typical examples are **quoting** a short passage for study, research, criticism or news, using works **for teaching** to an appropriate extent, making a **private copy** for personal use in some cases, and making a **back-up copy** of a legally owned program. Free use has conditions: the author's **name** and the **source** must be given, only a **justified amount** may be used, and the use must not harm the normal commercial use of the work. Copying a whole textbook "for study" is not free use.

The two ideas overlap but are not the same. **Plagiarism** is an **ethical** offence: not acknowledging the source. **Copyright infringement** is a **legal** offence: using a protected work without permission. Copying a public-domain poem without naming the poet is plagiarism but not infringement (no one owns it any more). Publishing a full licensed photo **with** the photographer's name but **without** permission is infringement but not plagiarism. Copying a protected article into your report without quotation marks and selling the report is **both**.

blocks.title: Worked example — a school website
blocks.content:
*Daniyar builds the website of the school robotics club. He wants to use (a) a photo from a news site, (b) a CC BY-NC image, (c) a quotation from an interview, (d) a JavaScript menu from GitHub under the MIT licence.*

1. **(a) News photo** — protected; no licence shown → he must **ask permission** or take his own photo.
2. **(b) CC BY-NC image** — allowed, because the club site is **non-commercial**; he must **credit the author** (BY).
3. **(c) Quotation** — allowed as **free use** if short, in quotation marks, with the **speaker and source** named.
4. **(d) MIT code** — allowed; the licence requires keeping the **copyright notice** in the code.

- Thinking that copyright must be **registered**, or that a work without © is free — protection is **automatic**.
- Thinking that everything on the Internet is in the **public domain**.
- Believing that crediting the author is enough to use **any** work — you also need **permission or a licence**.
- Saying that copyright protects **ideas** — it protects their **expression**.

theory.title: Software licences and using digital content legally

blocks.content: Software is the most common kind of protected work that students in Computer Science use every day — operating systems, office suites, libraries, games, images and fonts on websites. When you buy or download software you almost never buy the program itself; you receive a **licence** that says what you may and may not do with it. Knowing the main kinds of licence is part of knowing the copyright rules, and it is needed whenever you choose software for a new system or build a website for a client.

The **contract between the software owner and the user** that is accepted when the software is installed. It states **how many devices** may use it, whether it may be **copied, modified or resold**, and the owner's **liability**.

Software whose **source code is published** under a licence that allows anyone to **use, study, change and share** it, usually on condition that the licence and the authors' names are kept (e.g. **GPL**, **MIT**, **Apache**).

**Freeware** may be used **free of charge**, but the code is closed and it may not be changed or sold. **Shareware** may be **tried free** for a limited time or with limited features; after that the user must **pay** for a licence.

**Copying, installing, distributing or selling software without a valid licence** — for example, installing one licence on 30 school computers, or downloading a "cracked" copy. It is copyright infringement.

blocks.title: Kinds of software licence
rows: May the user give copies to others?
**Yes**, with the same licence (GPL) or with the notice (MIT)

blocks.content: Open-source licences come in two families. A **copyleft** licence such as the **GPL** says: you may use, change and share this code, but any program you **distribute** that includes it must also be released under the **GPL**, with its source code. The freedom is "passed on" to every later user. A **permissive** licence such as **MIT** or **Apache** asks only that you **keep the copyright notice** and the licence text; you may include the code even in a closed commercial product. When a developer builds a system for a client, the choice matters: putting GPL code into a closed product that is sold would break the licence, while MIT code can be used if the notice is kept.

blocks.text: Licences in a school or company

blocks.content: An organisation must keep a record of the licences it owns and make sure that the number of installations does not exceed them. A **single-user licence** covers one person or device; a **multi-user (volume) licence** covers a stated number; a **site licence** covers every computer at one site, such as a whole school; a **subscription** gives the right to use the software only while payments continue. Installing more copies than the licence allows is piracy even if the school paid for some of them.

blocks.title: Worked example — choosing software for the school robotics club
blocks.content:
*The robotics club has 15 laptops and no budget. It needs an office suite for its reports, an image editor for its website and a programming environment. A student suggests downloading a "cracked" copy of a paid image editor.*

1. **Cracked copy** — illegal (software piracy); it may also contain **malware**. Rejected.
2. **Office suite** — **LibreOffice** (open source, free, may be installed on all 15 laptops).
3. **Image editor** — **GIMP** (open source) or a freeware editor whose licence allows **non-commercial / educational** use; read the licence for the number of devices.
4. **Programming** — **Python** and **Thonny** (open source).
5. **Club website** — images under **CC BY**: credit each author on the page; icons from a library under the **MIT** licence: keep the notice in the code.
6. Record every program and its licence in the club's **licence register**.

- "Free" means "no copyright" — freeware is free to **use**, but it is still protected: you may not change or sell it.
- "Open source" means "no rules" — open-source licences have **conditions** (keep the notice; GPL: share changes under the GPL).
- Buying one licence and installing it on the whole class.
- Thinking that a **trial** licence of shareware may be used for ever by reinstalling it.

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name two copyright protection rules. [2]**
Any two: copyright arises **automatically** when the work is created (1); copying / publishing needs the **owner's permission / licence** (1); quotations must name the **author and source**; protection lasts for the author's **life + 70 years**; ideas are not protected, only their expression.

**Q: Explain the difference between quoting and paraphrasing. [2]**
A quotation uses the **exact words** in quotation marks (1); a paraphrase restates the idea **in your own words**; both need a citation (1).

**Q: A student finds a photograph on a website and wants to use it in a project report. Describe what the student must do to use it legally. [3]**
Check the **licence / terms** of the photo (1); if it is not free (e.g. no CC licence), ask the **owner for permission** (1); follow the licence conditions and **credit / cite** the author and source (1).

**Q: Explain why copyright protects software. [2]**
Software is an **original creative work** of its authors (1); without protection it could be copied and sold freely, and the authors would lose income / control (1).

**Q: State what is meant by the public domain. [1]**
Works no longer protected by copyright / free for anyone to use (1).

- Mixing up **plagiarism** (an ethical / academic problem: not acknowledging the source) and **copyright infringement** (a legal problem: using without permission). Both can happen at once.
- "Copyright lasts forever" — it lasts for a **limited time**.
- Answering "paraphrasing means changing some words" — the whole idea is rewritten **and** cited.
